# CloudFront and Global Accelerator: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=cloudfront-q011 -->
### Question 1

A company runs a payments API on Amazon EC2 instances behind Application Load Balancers in us-east-1 and us-west-2. Partner companies call the API with HTTPS POST requests. The firewalls of the partners allow outbound traffic only to IP addresses on an allow list, and the partners update their lists rarely. If the API fails in one Region, partner traffic must move automatically to another Region. Which solution will provide the FASTEST failover between the Regions?

- Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with an endpoint group in each Region for the Application Load Balancer of that Region, and give its static IP addresses to the partners.
- Place a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses in front of each Application Load Balancer, and create Amazon Route 53 failover records with health checks for the Network Load Balancers.
- Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an origin group that contains both Application Load Balancers, and fail over to the us-west-2 load balancer on 5xx status codes.
- Attach Elastic IP addresses to the Application Load Balancer in each Region, and create Amazon Route 53 weighted records with health checks that point to those addresses.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with an endpoint group in each Region for the Application Load Balancer of that Region, and give its static IP addresses to the partners.

**Deciding phrases.** "HTTPS POST requests", "allow outbound traffic only to IP addresses on an allow list", "FASTEST failover"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the FASTEST failover between the Regions.
2. I mark the constraints: the partners send HTTPS POST requests, their firewalls allow only listed IP addresses, and traffic must move automatically to another Region.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a CloudFront distribution with an origin group, because an origin group switches to a second origin without a person.
4. I remove the Elastic IP addresses on the Application Load Balancers, because in the feature table only the Network Load Balancer has static or Elastic IP addresses.
5. Between the CloudFront origin group and Global Accelerator, the difference is the request method and the addresses. My first idea breaks because CloudFront fails over only GET, HEAD and OPTIONS requests, and the partners send POST requests. The Route 53 option works, but resolvers keep old answers until their TTL runs out.
6. Check: Global Accelerator gives two static IP addresses for the allow list, moves traffic to the healthy Region, and does not wait for DNS caches. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The partners need fixed addresses, and a DNS-based failover waits for caches. With Global Accelerator you do not depend on [the IP address caching settings of client devices](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-no-dns-cache-dependency-seconds), and [change propagation takes a matter of seconds](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-no-dns-cache-dependency-seconds). The partners keep calling the same two addresses while traffic moves to the healthy Region.

**Why not.**

- "Place a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP ...": It works, but resolvers cache DNS answers [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control), so some partners keep calling the failed Region until the cached answer expires.
- "Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an origin ...": The partners send POST requests, and CloudFront fails over [only when the HTTP method of the viewer](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-failover-only-get-head-options) request is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS.
- "Attach Elastic IP addresses to the Application Load ...": In the Elastic Load Balancing feature table, [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) is a feature of the Network Load Balancer, not of the Application Load Balancer.

**Twin.** If the stem said "partners resolve a DNS name and accept several minutes of downtime" instead: DNS failover records are enough, because a wait [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control) is acceptable.

**Takeaway.** Fixed IP addresses and fast Region failover for POST traffic: AWS Global Accelerator.

**Review.** [Global Accelerator carries TCP and UDP from two static addresses over the AWS network](2-deep.md#global-accelerator-carries-tcp-and-udp-from-two-static-addresses-over-the-aws-network-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs a single-page web application from an Amazon S3 bucket through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The team deploys new JavaScript and CSS files several times each day under the same file names. After each deployment, some users keep running the old files, including users whose browser or corporate proxy kept a copy. The team creates invalidations for the changed files after each deployment, and the invalidation charges grow every month. Users must get the new files right after each deployment. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Keep the current file names, and create one invalidation for the /* path after each deployment, because a wildcard path counts as one invalidation path.
- Turn on S3 Versioning for the origin bucket, so that each deployment stores a new object version that CloudFront serves to users after the upload.
- Add a version identifier to the JavaScript and CSS file names in each deployment, give index.html a short TTL, and give the versioned files a long TTL.
- Set a Cache-Control max-age of 0 seconds on every file in the bucket, so that CloudFront, browsers and proxies revalidate each file with the origin on every request.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a version identifier to the JavaScript and CSS file names in each deployment, give index.html a short TTL, and give the versioned files a long TTL.

**Deciding phrases.** "under the same file names", "browser or corporate proxy kept a copy", "MOST cost-effective"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective way to give users the new files right after each deployment.
2. I mark the constraints: the file names stay the same, browsers and corporate proxies keep copies, the invalidation charges grow, and users need the new files right after each deployment.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict versioned file names, because a new name is a new URL that no cache holds yet.
4. I remove the /* invalidation, because it clears the CloudFront caches but not the browsers or the proxies. I remove S3 Versioning, because it is not related to CloudFront file versioning.
5. Between versioned names and a max-age of 0 seconds, the difference is the number of origin requests; the stem asks for the lowest cost, so revalidating every request loses.
6. Check: versioned names reach browsers, proxies and edge caches, need no invalidation, and keep long TTLs for the files. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Old copies live in edge caches, browsers and corporate proxies. A new file name is a new URL, so every cache fetches the new file, and index.html with a short TTL points to it. AWS says to [use invalidation only in unexpected circumstances](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-invalidate-only-unexpected-use-versioning) and to [implement a versioning system for your files](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-invalidate-only-unexpected-use-versioning).

**Why not.**

- "Keep the current file names, and create one ...": The wildcard [counts as one path](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-invalidation-wildcard-counts-one-path), but invalidation clears the CloudFront caches, not the copies that browsers and corporate proxies keep.
- "Turn on S3 Versioning for the origin bucket, ...": CloudFront file versioning [is not related to Amazon S3 object versioning](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-versioning-not-s3-versioning); the file names stay the same, so cached copies stay old.
- "Set a Cache-Control max-age of 0 seconds on ...": It works, but with [0 seconds](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-expiration-zero-seconds-revalidates) CloudFront will [revalidate every request with the origin server](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-expiration-zero-seconds-revalidates), so every page load pays for origin requests.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a file with wrong prices must disappear from the edge caches now" instead: create an invalidation, because AWS says to [use invalidation only in unexpected circumstances](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-invalidate-only-unexpected-use-versioning) like this one.

**Takeaway.** Frequent releases behind CloudFront: change the file names, not the cache.

**Review.** [Cache headers decide how long a copy lives and versioned names replace it sooner](2-deep.md#cache-headers-decide-how-long-a-copy-lives-and-versioned-names-replace-it-sooner-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company sells furniture online. Its product pages load images from one Amazon S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region, and the images change only a few times each year. The company now has users around the world. Users in Asia and Europe report that product pages load slowly because each image takes a long time to download. The company wants to reduce the time that these users wait for the images. What should a solutions architect recommend?

- Launch Amazon EC2 instances in the edge locations near users in Asia and Europe, and copy the product images to the instances.
- Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as its origin, and load the product images through the domain name of the distribution.
- Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with the S3 bucket as its endpoint, so that edge locations keep copies of the images.
- Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket, and load the product images through the accelerated endpoint name of the bucket.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as its origin, and load the product images through the domain name of the distribution.

**Deciding phrases.** "users around the world", "the images change only a few times each year", "takes a long time to download"

**Why.** The images rarely change and the users are far from us-east-1, so the fix is a cache near the users. CloudFront suits [frequently accessed static content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-good-for-static-edge-content), and each request goes to the [edge location that provides the lowest latency](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-request-routed-lowest-latency-edge). After the first request for an image, CloudFront [adds the object to the cache](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-first-byte-forwarded-and-cached) for the next request, so later users wait less.

**Why not.**

- "Launch Amazon EC2 instances in the edge locations ...": Edge locations run AWS services, not your instances: [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon Route 53, AWS Firewall Manager, AWS Shield, and AWS WAF services are provided through AWS Edge Locations](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-edge-location-services).
- "Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with ...": Global Accelerator works by [proxying packets at the edge](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-vs-cloudfront-content-types), and its endpoints are [Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-standard-endpoint-types), EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses.
- "Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket, ...": Transfer Acceleration is for customers who [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use), and [no data is ever saved](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-no-data-at-edge) at the edge, so each image still comes from us-east-1.

**Twin.** If the stem said "customers upload large videos to the bucket from many countries" instead: S3 Transfer Acceleration, because it is for customers who [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use).

**Takeaway.** Static files and users far from the bucket: put a CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket.

**Review.** [Requests reach the nearest edge location and cache misses travel on to the origin](2-deep.md#requests-reach-the-nearest-edge-location-and-cache-misses-travel-on-to-the-origin-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company serves a static website from an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1 through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Visitors read pages and download files, and they never upload anything. S3 Cross-Region Replication copies every object to a second bucket in us-west-2. The website must stay highly available if the us-east-1 bucket starts to return server errors during a Regional problem. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the 5xx error rate of the distribution, and let the alarm start a script that changes the origin of the distribution to the us-west-2 bucket.
- Associate a Lambda@Edge function with the origin response event, and let the function fetch the file from the us-west-2 bucket when the us-east-1 bucket returns an error.
- Create an origin group that fails over from the us-east-1 bucket to the us-west-2 bucket on 5xx status codes, and use the group in the default cache behavior.
- Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with both buckets as endpoints, and let its health checks move the traffic to the us-west-2 bucket.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an origin group that fails over from the us-east-1 bucket to the us-west-2 bucket on 5xx status codes, and use the group in the default cache behavior.

**Deciding phrases.** "copies every object to a second bucket in us-west-2", "return server errors", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Origin failover is built into CloudFront. It needs [a distribution with at least two origins](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-failover-needs-two-origins), an origin group, and a cache behavior that uses the group. When the primary origin fails or returns one of the chosen status codes, [CloudFront automatically switches to the secondary origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-failover-switches-to-secondary). No person and no code acts during the outage.

**Why not.**

- "Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the 5xx ...": It works, but edits made during an outage [depend on the CloudFront control plane](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-static-stability-use-origin-failover-not-manual), and the alarm and the script are more parts to run.
- "Associate a Lambda@Edge function with the origin response ...": It works, because Lambda@Edge can [make network calls to external resources](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-network-calls-allowed), but it is code to write and maintain for a retry that CloudFront offers as a setting.
- "Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with ...": Accelerator endpoints are [Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-standard-endpoint-types), EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses, so an S3 bucket cannot be one.

**Twin.** If the stem said "visitors also upload files with PUT requests" instead: the uploads would not fail over, because CloudFront fails over [only when the HTTP method of the viewer](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-failover-only-get-head-options) request is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS.

**Takeaway.** A replica origin behind CloudFront: use an origin group, not a script or edge code.

**Review.** [An origin group fails over to a second origin when the first one fails](2-deep.md#an-origin-group-fails-over-to-a-second-origin-when-the-first-one-fails-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A news company serves its website to millions of readers through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin is a group of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in one AWS Region. Most page requests are served from the CloudFront cache. A new feature needs a small piece of logic that runs for every viewer request. Each request must be rewritten to a language folder, such as /de/, based on the Accept-Language header of the request. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Write the logic as a CloudFront function, and associate the function with the viewer request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
- Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and associate the function with the viewer request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
- Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and associate the function with the origin request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
- Attach the managed CachingDisabled cache policy to the default cache behavior, and add the logic to the application that runs on the EC2 instances.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Write the logic as a CloudFront function, and associate the function with the viewer request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.

**Deciding phrases.** "rewritten to a language folder", "Most page requests are served from the CloudFront cache", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** A URL rewrite is light work that needs no network call, and CloudFront Functions suit [URL redirects or rewrites](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-use-cases). The function rewrites the path at the edge on the viewer request, so each language folder gets its own cached copy. CloudFront Functions cost [a fraction of the price of AWS Lambda@Edge](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-functions-cheaper-than-lambda-edge).

**Why not.**

- "Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and ...": It works, but Lambda@Edge costs more for the same rewrite: CloudFront Functions cost [a fraction of the price of AWS Lambda@Edge](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-functions-cheaper-than-lambda-edge).
- "Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and ...": When the page is in the cache, [the function doesn't execute](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-origin-request-only-on-miss), so cached pages skip the rewrite and readers get another language.
- "Attach the managed CachingDisabled cache policy to the ...": It works, but [this policy disables caching](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled), so every request reaches the EC2 instances, which costs far more than a rewrite at the edge.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Each request must be checked against a list of blocked reader accounts in an Amazon DynamoDB table" instead: a Lambda@Edge function, because it can [make network calls to external resources](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-network-calls-allowed).

**Takeaway.** Light URL or header work on every request: a CloudFront function on the viewer request event.

**Review.** [CloudFront Functions do light rewrites and edge Lambda functions can call other services](2-deep.md#cloudfront-functions-do-light-rewrites-and-edge-lambda-functions-can-call-other-services-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company distributes installers for its desktop software from an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1. Users around the world download the installers directly from the bucket, and each new version is downloaded millions of times in its first week. Users far from us-east-1 report slow downloads, and the data transfer charges of the bucket keep growing. The company must reduce download times and keep data transfer costs low. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Replicate the bucket to S3 buckets in Europe and Asia with S3 Cross-Region Replication, and send each user to the nearest bucket instead of paying CloudFront transfer charges.
- Move the installers to Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer, and put an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator in front of the load balancer.
- Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket, and change the download links to use the accelerated endpoint name of the bucket.
- Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the bucket as its origin, and change the download links to use the domain name of the distribution.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the bucket as its origin, and change the download links to use the domain name of the distribution.

**Deciding phrases.** "downloaded millions of times", "keep data transfer costs low", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Each installer is downloaded millions of times, so edge caches can answer most downloads. CloudFront suits [frequently accessed static content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-good-for-static-edge-content). Amazon S3 does not charge for [data transferred out to Amazon CloudFront](../facts/s3.md#s3-pricing-data-transfer-to-cloudfront-free), and the company pays for [the outbound data transfer from CloudFront](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-price-origin-to-cloudfront-always-free-aws-origins) to the users.

**Why not.**

- "Replicate the bucket to S3 buckets in Europe ...": Each regional bucket still serves every download without a cache, and the copies add storage and replication charges, while the fetch from S3 to CloudFront is [always free when using AWS origins](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-price-origin-to-cloudfront-always-free-aws-origins).
- "Move the installers to Amazon EC2 instances behind ...": It works for speed, but an accelerator adds [a fixed hourly fee](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-price-fixed-hourly-fee-plus-dt-premium) and a [Data Transfer-Premium fee (DT-Premium)](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-price-fixed-hourly-fee-plus-dt-premium), and nothing is cached.
- "Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket, ...": Transfer Acceleration is for customers who [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use), and [no data is ever saved](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-no-data-at-edge) at the edge, so every download still leaves the bucket.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the installers are served by EC2 instances behind a load balancer" instead: CloudFront still fits, because transfer from Elastic Load Balancing is also [always free when using AWS origins](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-price-origin-to-cloudfront-always-free-aws-origins).

**Takeaway.** Popular downloads for users far away: CloudFront in front of the bucket is faster, and the origin fetch is free.

**Review.** [CloudFront bills data sent to viewers and Global Accelerator adds an hourly fee](2-deep.md#cloudfront-bills-data-sent-to-viewers-and-global-accelerator-adds-an-hourly-fee-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A news company serves its website to millions of readers through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin is a group of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in one AWS Region. Most page requests are served from the CloudFront cache. A new feature needs a small piece of logic that runs for every viewer request. Each request must be checked against a list of blocked reader accounts in an Amazon DynamoDB table, and blocked readers must get an error page. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Write the logic as a CloudFront function, and associate the function with the viewer request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
- Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and associate the function with the viewer request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
- Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and associate the function with the origin request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
- Attach the managed CachingDisabled cache policy to the default cache behavior, and add the logic to the application that runs on the EC2 instances.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and associate the function with the viewer request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.

**Deciding phrases.** "checked against a list of blocked reader accounts in an Amazon DynamoDB table", "Most page requests are served from the CloudFront cache", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The check needs a call to DynamoDB on every request, cached pages included. Lambda@Edge can [make network calls to external resources](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-network-calls-allowed), and a viewer request trigger runs [when CloudFront receives a request from a viewer](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-viewer-request-before-cache), before the cache check. CloudFront Functions are cheaper, but they have no [network access](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-no-network-no-body-fs-access).

**Why not.**

- "Write the logic as a CloudFront function, and ...": CloudFront Functions have no [network access](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-no-network-no-body-fs-access), so the function cannot read the list in the DynamoDB table.
- "Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and ...": When the page is in the cache, [the function doesn't execute](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-origin-request-only-on-miss), so blocked readers still get cached pages.
- "Attach the managed CachingDisabled cache policy to the ...": It works, but [this policy disables caching](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled), so every request reaches the EC2 instances, which costs far more than a check at the edge.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Each request must be rewritten to a language folder, such as /de/, based on the Accept-Language header of the request" instead: a CloudFront function, because it suits [URL redirects or rewrites](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-use-cases).

**Takeaway.** Edge logic that calls another service on every request: Lambda@Edge on the viewer request event.

**Review.** [CloudFront Functions do light rewrites and edge Lambda functions can call other services](2-deep.md#cloudfront-functions-do-light-rewrites-and-edge-lambda-functions-can-call-other-services-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company serves an online store at shop.example.com through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin is an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in eu-central-1, and the distribution reaches it at origin.example.com. The viewer protocol policy redirects HTTP to HTTPS, and the distribution uses an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate for shop.example.com. A security review finds that the load balancer has only an HTTP listener. The company must ensure that data is encrypted in transit all the way to the load balancer. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Change the viewer protocol policy to HTTPS Only, so that CloudFront refuses HTTP requests from viewers and keeps each request encrypted on its way to the load balancer.
- Configure field-level encryption for the form fields that hold customer data, so that CloudFront encrypts those fields before it forwards each request to the load balancer.
- Replace the load balancer with a Network Load Balancer that passes TCP port 443 to the instances, and install a certificate from a third-party authority on each instance.
- Request an ACM certificate for origin.example.com in eu-central-1, add an HTTPS listener with it to the load balancer, and set the origin protocol policy to HTTPS only.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Request an ACM certificate for origin.example.com in eu-central-1, add an HTTPS listener with it to the load balancer, and set the origin protocol policy to HTTPS only.

**Deciding phrases.** "the load balancer has only an HTTP listener", "encrypted in transit all the way to the load balancer", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Encryption in transit through CloudFront has two settings: [require that viewers use HTTPS](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-encrypt-in-transit-viewer-and-origin-https), which the redirect already does, and [use HTTPS to get files from your origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-encrypt-in-transit-viewer-and-origin-https). The load balancer needs an HTTPS listener whose ACM certificate [must be in the same Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the load balancer.

**Why not.**

- "Change the viewer protocol policy to HTTPS Only, ...": The two legs are separate settings: CloudFront serves objects [regardless of whether the protocol used](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-https-viewer-origin-protocol-independent) toward the origin matches the viewer's, so the origin leg stays HTTP.
- "Configure field-level encryption for the form fields that ...": Field-level encryption [adds an additional layer of security](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-fle-layer-on-https-selected-fields) for chosen fields on top of HTTPS; the rest of each request still crosses the origin leg over HTTP.
- "Replace the load balancer with a Network Load ...": It works, but it replaces the load balancer and puts third-party certificates on every instance, while for ACM certificates [ACM manages certificate renewals for you](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cert-acm-managed-renewal).

**Twin.** If the stem said "the viewer protocol policy allows HTTP and HTTPS" instead: also set it to Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, because then [HTTP requests are automatically redirected to HTTPS requests](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-vpp-redirect-http-to-https).

**Takeaway.** CloudFront encrypts two legs with two settings: the viewer protocol policy and the origin protocol policy.

**Review.** [CloudFront encrypts two separate connections and each one has its own setting](2-deep.md#cloudfront-encrypts-two-separate-connections-and-each-one-has-its-own-setting-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company sells online courses. It stores the course files in an Amazon S3 bucket and delivers them to learners through an Amazon CloudFront distribution in the same AWS account. A solutions architect must restrict access to the course files. Every visitor of the website can download the files, but nobody can download them with Amazon S3 URLs. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Configure origin access control on the S3 origin, and add a bucket policy that allows the CloudFront service principal to read objects for this distribution only.
- Add a trusted key group to the cache behavior, and have the application create a CloudFront signed URL for each file after the user signs in.
- Add a bucket policy that allows public reads of the objects for requests that carry the domain name of the website in the Referer header.
- Serve the files through an application on Amazon EC2 instances that checks each request and reads the objects from the bucket with an IAM role.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Configure origin access control on the S3 origin, and add a bucket policy that allows the CloudFront service principal to read objects for this distribution only.

**Deciding phrases.** "Every visitor of the website can download the files", "nobody can download them with Amazon S3 URLs", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The stem restricts the path, not the users: every visitor can download. With origin access control, the bucket policy allows CloudFront [only when the request is on behalf](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal) of this distribution, so the bucket stays private.

**Why not.**

- "Add a trusted key group to the cache ...": Signed URLs check users, which the stem does not need, and they leave S3 URLs working; locking the bucket is a separate step: [this prevents someone from bypassing CloudFront](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-private-s3-oac-plus-signed-urls).
- "Add a bucket policy that allows public reads ...": A public read policy makes S3 URLs work for anyone who sends that header, and CloudFront needs no public access: the policy can allow the [CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal).
- "Serve the files through an application on Amazon ...": It works, but the company then runs and scales instances for every download, while origin access control is one setting plus a bucket policy.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Only customers who paid for a course can download its files, for a limited time" instead: CloudFront signed URLs, because they serve [users who have paid a fee](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-signed-urls-cookies-for-paying-users).

**Takeaway.** Stop S3 URLs with origin access control; choose which users get files with signed URLs or signed cookies.

**Review.** [Origin access control keeps the bucket private and lets your distribution read it](2-deep.md#origin-access-control-keeps-the-bucket-private-and-lets-your-distribution-read-it-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=cloudfront-q010 -->
### Question 10

A company sells online courses. It stores the course files in an Amazon S3 bucket and delivers them to learners through an Amazon CloudFront distribution in the same AWS account. A solutions architect must restrict access to the course files. Only customers who paid for a course can download its files, for a limited time. The bucket already accepts reads only from the distribution through origin access control. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Configure origin access control on the S3 origin, and add a bucket policy that allows the CloudFront service principal to read objects for this distribution only.
- Add a trusted key group to the cache behavior, and have the application create a CloudFront signed URL for each file after the user signs in.
- Add a bucket policy that allows public reads of the objects for requests that carry the domain name of the website in the Referer header.
- Serve the files through an application on Amazon EC2 instances that checks each request and reads the objects from the bucket with an IAM role.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a trusted key group to the cache behavior, and have the application create a CloudFront signed URL for each file after the user signs in.

**Deciding phrases.** "Only customers who paid for a course", "for a limited time", "The bucket already accepts reads only from the distribution"

**Why.** The bucket is already private, so the open need is per user and per time. CloudFront restricts content to selected users by [using signed URLs or signed cookies](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-signed-urls-cookies-for-paying-users). The application signs each URL after sign-in with [a trusted key group that you create](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signer-key-group-recommended), and CloudFront checks the signature before it serves the file.

**Why not.**

- "Configure origin access control on the S3 origin, ...": Origin access control is already in place; it makes sure that [only CloudFront can access the content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-secure-origin-oac-supported-origins), and it does not know which customers paid.
- "Add a bucket policy that allows public reads ...": A public read policy undoes origin access control: anyone who sends that header can then use S3 URLs, whether the person paid or not.
- "Serve the files through an application on Amazon ...": It works, because the application can check each payment, but the company then runs a fleet for downloads that CloudFront can check at the edge.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Every visitor of the website can download the files, but nobody can download them with Amazon S3 URLs" instead: origin access control, because then viewers [cannot access it directly by using Amazon S3 URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-private-s3-oac-plus-signed-urls).

**Takeaway.** Stop S3 URLs with origin access control; choose which users get files with signed URLs or signed cookies.

**Review.** [Signed URLs and signed cookies decide which users can fetch private files](2-deep.md#signed-urls-and-signed-cookies-decide-which-users-can-fetch-private-files-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

## Extended

<!-- quiz:start id=cloudfront-q009 -->
### Question 11

A company hosts the static assets of a web application in an Amazon S3 bucket. The API of the application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The browser sends API calls to paths that start with /api/, and every other path is a static asset. All requests must use one domain name. Static assets must be cached at edge locations, and API responses must not be cached. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create two CloudFront distributions, one with the bucket as its origin and one with the load balancer as its origin, and give each distribution its own domain name.
- Copy the static assets to the EC2 instances, and create one CloudFront distribution with the load balancer as its origin and a /api/* behavior that uses CachingDisabled.
- Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with the bucket and the load balancer as endpoints, and send the /api/ paths to the load balancer endpoint.
- Create one CloudFront distribution with both origins, a /api/* cache behavior for the load balancer with CachingDisabled, and a default cache behavior for the bucket.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create one CloudFront distribution with both origins, a /api/* cache behavior for the load balancer with CachingDisabled, and a default cache behavior for the bucket.

**Deciding phrases.** "All requests must use one domain name", "API responses must not be cached", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** One distribution can hold both origins, because in each cache behavior [you specify the one origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-behavior-one-origin-each). CloudFront compares the path with the behaviors in order, and [the first match determines which cache behavior](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-behavior-first-match-wins) applies. The /api/* behavior uses CachingDisabled, and [this policy disables caching](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled). The default behavior serves the bucket from the edge caches.

**Why not.**

- "Create two CloudFront distributions, one with the bucket ...": It breaks the one-domain requirement, and one distribution can serve both origins, because [you specify the one origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-behavior-one-origin-each) in each cache behavior.
- "Copy the static assets to the EC2 instances, ...": It works, but the instances then store, deploy and serve every asset, which is more work than keeping the bucket as a second origin.
- "Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with ...": Accelerator endpoints are [Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-standard-endpoint-types), EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses, so the bucket cannot be one.

**Twin.** If the stem said "API responses can be cached for a few seconds" instead: keep both behaviors, but give the /api/* behavior a cache policy with a short time to live (TTL) in place of CachingDisabled.

**Takeaway.** Two origins under one domain name: one distribution, with one cache behavior for each path pattern.

**Review.** [Cache behaviors send each URL path to one origin and the first match wins](2-deep.md#cache-behaviors-send-each-url-path-to-one-origin-and-the-first-match-wins-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=cloudfront-q021 -->
### Question 12

A company runs an online course website. Each course video uses HLS, so the video is split into hundreds of small segment files that the player requests one after another. The files are served through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Only signed-in subscribers can watch, and each subscriber must get temporary access to all files of a video. The company does not want to change the URLs that the video player requests. What should the company use to control access?

- A CloudFront signed URL for each segment file, which the website creates for a subscriber after sign-in
- CloudFront geographic restriction that allows the countries where the subscribers of the company live
- CloudFront signed cookies, which the website sets for a subscriber after sign-in, with an expiration time for the access
- An AWS WAF web ACL on the distribution that allows the IP addresses of signed-in subscribers

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** CloudFront signed cookies, which the website sets for a subscriber after sign-in, with an expiration time for the access

**Deciding phrases.** "hundreds of small segment files", "temporary access to all files of a video", "does not want to change the URLs"

**Why.** Signed cookies fit two parts of the stem: they give [access to multiple restricted files](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signed-cookies-when-multiple-files-or-keep-urls), such as every segment of one video, and they work when [you don't want to change your current URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signed-cookies-when-multiple-files-or-keep-urls). The website sets an expiration time in the cookies, so the access is temporary.

**Why not.**

- "A CloudFront signed URL for each segment file, ...": Signed URLs fit when you [restrict access to individual files](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signed-url-when-individual-files-or-no-cookies); hundreds of segments need hundreds of new URLs, so the URLs change.
- "CloudFront geographic restriction that allows the countries where ...": [Geographic restrictions apply to an entire distribution](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-geo-restriction-country-level-whole-distribution) at the country level, so anyone in an allowed country can watch.
- "An AWS WAF web ACL on the distribution ...": Subscribers change networks and share addresses, so an IP allow list does not follow the person who paid, and it has no expiration time.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each subscriber downloads one PDF certificate" instead: a signed URL, because signed URLs fit when you [restrict access to individual files](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signed-url-when-individual-files-or-no-cookies).

**Takeaway.** Many private files for one user and URLs that stay the same: CloudFront signed cookies.

**Review.** [Signed URLs and signed cookies decide which users can fetch private files](2-deep.md#signed-urls-and-signed-cookies-decide-which-users-can-fetch-private-files-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=cloudfront-q005 -->
### Question 13

A company runs a product catalog website on Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Viewers are in many countries. The cache hit ratio is low, and the origin instances are overloaded. The cache policy of the distribution includes all query strings, all cookies and the User-Agent header in the cache key. Each catalog page changes only with the value of the lang query string. The team does not want to write or maintain any code for this change. Which combination of steps will raise the cache hit ratio and reduce the origin load with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Attach a cache policy to the cache behavior that includes only the lang query string in the cache key, with no cookies and no headers.
- Associate a CloudFront function with the viewer request event that removes all cookies, the User-Agent header and every query string except lang.
- Keep all cookies in the cache key, and add every other viewer header to it, so that each cached copy matches its request more exactly.
- Turn on Origin Shield for the origin, and choose the AWS Region that has the lowest latency to the EC2 instances of the catalog.
- Create an invalidation for the /* path every hour, so that the edge locations keep a fresh copy of every catalog page.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Attach a cache policy to the cache behavior that includes only the lang query string in the cache key, with no cookies and no headers.
- Turn on Origin Shield for the origin, and choose the AWS Region that has the lowest latency to the EC2 instances of the catalog.

**Deciding phrases.** "changes only with the value of the lang query string", "the origin instances are overloaded", "does not want to write or maintain any code", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Values in the cache key that do not change the page split it into many separate copies. A cache policy decides what is [included in the cache key](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cache-policy-controls-cache-key), so a key with only lang raises the hit ratio. With Origin Shield, CloudFront will [route all origin fetches through Origin Shield](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-origin-shield-central-cache-layer), one more cache before the origin.

- AWS says to [forward only the query string parameters](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cache-hit-ratio-forward-only-needed-values) that change the response.
- Origin Shield is a [centralized caching layer](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-origin-shield-central-cache-layer), placed in [the AWS Region that has the lowest latency](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-origin-shield-choose-lowest-latency-region) to the origin.

**Why not.**

- "Associate a CloudFront function with the viewer request ...": It works, because [cache key normalization](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-use-cases) suits CloudFront Functions, but it is code to write and maintain where a policy setting is enough.
- "Keep all cookies in the cache key, and ...": Every extra value splits a page into more copies; AWS says to [forward only specified cookies instead of forwarding all](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cache-hit-ratio-forward-only-needed-values) cookies.
- "Create an invalidation for the /* path every ...": An invalidation empties the cache, so the next requests go to the origin; AWS says to [use invalidation only in unexpected circumstances](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-invalidate-only-unexpected-use-versioning).

**Twin.** If the stem said "every page is different for each signed-in user" instead: the pages are not cacheable, and the managed CachingDisabled policy is [useful for dynamic content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled).

**Takeaway.** Low hit ratio: shrink the cache key to the values that change the page, then add Origin Shield.

**Review.** [The cache key decides which requests share one cached copy](2-deep.md#the-cache-key-decides-which-requests-share-one-cached-copy-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=cloudfront-q017 -->
### Question 14

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The load balancer is internet-facing in public subnets. An Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the load balancer caches static pages at edge locations near users. A security review requires that the load balancer is no longer internet-facing and that users reach the application only through CloudFront. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Keep the internet-facing load balancer in the public subnets, and allow inbound traffic in its security group only from the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront.
- Create an internal Application Load Balancer in private subnets for the instances, and add the internal load balancer to the distribution as a VPC origin.
- Create an internal Application Load Balancer in private subnets, and run proxy instances in public subnets that accept traffic from CloudFront and forward it to the load balancer.
- Keep the current load balancer as the origin, and attach origin access control to the load balancer origin so that it accepts signed CloudFront requests.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an internal Application Load Balancer in private subnets for the instances, and add the internal load balancer to the distribution as a VPC origin.

**Deciding phrases.** "no longer internet-facing", "only through CloudFront", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** VPC origins let CloudFront use an [Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer, or EC2 instance in a private subnet](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-origin-private-subnet-vpc-origin). The internal load balancer has no internet entry point, and CloudFront becomes the one way in. Static pages still come from the edge caches, so caching does not change.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the internet-facing load balancer in the public ...": The security group blocks other callers, but the load balancer stays internet-facing, which the security review forbids.
- "Create an internal Application Load Balancer in private ...": It works, but the proxy instances are more servers to patch, scale and protect; a VPC origin reaches the load balancer [over a private, secure connection](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-vpc-origin-cloudfront-single-entry-point).
- "Keep the current load balancer as the origin, ...": Origin access control restricts [Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) Origins, AWS Elemental Origins, and Lambda Function URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-secure-origin-oac-supported-origins), and a load balancer is not one of them.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the load balancer must stay internet-facing until next quarter" instead: limit its security group to the [AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg), so that other callers are blocked.

**Takeaway.** A private load balancer behind CloudFront: make it internal and add it as a VPC origin.

**Review.** [VPC origins let CloudFront reach load balancers and instances in private subnets](2-deep.md#vpc-origins-let-cloudfront-reach-load-balancers-and-instances-in-private-subnets-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=cloudfront-q008 -->
### Question 15

A company runs a banking API behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin returns account balances with the header Cache-Control: no-cache. The /api/* cache behavior uses a custom cache policy, created by a former team member, with a Minimum TTL of 3600 seconds. After a payment, users see their old balance for up to an hour. Each balance request must return the current balance. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Keep the cache policy as it is, and change the origin so that each balance response also carries the Cache-Control directives no-store and private.
- Change the mobile and web clients to add a unique query string value to each balance request, and include all query strings in the cache key.
- Edit the custom cache policy of the /api/* cache behavior, and set its Minimum TTL to 0 seconds so that the origin's headers decide caching.
- Change the mobile and web clients to send the header Cache-Control: no-cache with each balance request, so that CloudFront fetches a fresh copy from the origin.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Edit the custom cache policy of the /api/* cache behavior, and set its Minimum TTL to 0 seconds so that the origin's headers decide caching.

**Deciding phrases.** "Cache-Control: no-cache", "Minimum TTL of 3600 seconds", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The origin already sends no-cache, but the cache policy sets a floor. If the [minimum TTL is greater than 0](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache), CloudFront caches for at least that time, even when the origin sends no-cache, [no-store, or private](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache). A Minimum TTL of 0 removes the floor with one change in the policy.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the cache policy as it is, and ...": CloudFront keeps the Minimum TTL even when the origin sends no-cache, [no-store, or private](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache), so more directives change nothing while the floor stays.
- "Change the mobile and web clients to add ...": It works, because every request gets its own cache key, but it changes every client and fills the cache with single-use copies.
- "Change the mobile and web clients to send ...": [CloudFront ignores those header fields in viewer requests](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-expiration-viewer-cache-control-ignored), so a viewer cannot force a trip to the origin while the cached copy is still valid.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the origin sends no Cache-Control header, and the Default TTL is 3600 seconds" instead: lower the Default TTL, because CloudFront uses it [as the object's TTL](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-ttl-default-ttl-only-without-headers) when no such header arrives.

**Takeaway.** Stale content although the origin says no-cache: check the Minimum TTL of the cache policy first.

**Review.** [Cache headers decide how long a copy lives and versioned names replace it sooner](2-deep.md#cache-headers-decide-how-long-a-copy-lives-and-versioned-names-replace-it-sooner-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=cloudfront-q012 -->
### Question 16

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. The load balancer is the origin of an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Attackers now send requests to the DNS name of the load balancer directly, which bypasses the protections at CloudFront. The load balancer must stay internet-facing until a network redesign next quarter. The load balancer must not accept connections from IP addresses outside CloudFront, and only requests that come through the company's own distribution may reach the application. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Configure origin access control on the load balancer origin, so that CloudFront signs each request and the load balancer rejects every request without a signature.
- In the security group of the load balancer, allow inbound HTTPS from the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront, and remove the other inbound rules.
- Add a deny rule to the network ACL of the load balancer subnets for each IP address that sends requests directly to the load balancer.
- Configure CloudFront to add a secret custom header to origin requests, and add a listener rule that forwards only the requests that carry that header.
- Run an AWS Lambda function each day that reads the published CloudFront IP ranges and rewrites the inbound rules of the security group of the load balancer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- In the security group of the load balancer, allow inbound HTTPS from the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront, and remove the other inbound rules.
- Configure CloudFront to add a secret custom header to origin requests, and add a listener rule that forwards only the requests that carry that header.

**Deciding phrases.** "must stay internet-facing", "must not accept connections from IP addresses outside CloudFront", "only requests that come through the company's own distribution", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Two locks work together on an internet-facing origin. The security group allows the [AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg), and AWS says to [remove any other inbound rules](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg). A secret header that CloudFront adds marks the requests of this distribution.

- The group then admits only the [AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg), which [prevents non-CloudFront traffic from reaching your origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-prefix-list-origin-facing-servers).
- CloudFront can [add a custom HTTP header to requests](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-alb-restrict-custom-header-and-https), and the listener can [only forward requests that contain the custom HTTP](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-alb-restrict-custom-header-and-https) header that marks this distribution.

**Why not.**

- "Configure origin access control on the load balancer ...": Origin access control covers Amazon Simple Storage Service ([S3) Origins, AWS Elemental Origins, and Lambda Function URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-secure-origin-oac-supported-origins), and a load balancer is not one of them.
- "Add a deny rule to the network ACL ...": A deny list blocks known addresses, and [you can't reference prefix lists in network ACL rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-nacl-no-prefix-lists), so a network ACL cannot admit CloudFront alone.
- "Run an AWS Lambda function each day that ...": It works, but it is code to run and fix, while [the CloudFront managed prefix list contains the IP](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-prefix-list-origin-facing-servers) ranges already and stays current.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the load balancer can move to private subnets now" instead: use a VPC origin, because CloudFront works with [internal Application Load Balancers inside private subnets](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-alb-internal-needs-vpc-origins).

**Takeaway.** Public load balancer behind CloudFront: prefix list in the security group plus a secret header. Private load balancer: VPC origin.

**Review.** [VPC origins let CloudFront reach load balancers and instances in private subnets](2-deep.md#vpc-origins-let-cloudfront-reach-load-balancers-and-instances-in-private-subnets-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=cloudfront-q014 -->
### Question 17

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in ap-southeast-2. The company adds an Amazon CloudFront distribution for www.example.com in front of the load balancer. Both connections, from viewers to CloudFront and from CloudFront to the load balancer, must use HTTPS so that data stays encrypted in transit. Both must use public certificates from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), and the load balancer will use a certificate for origin.example.com. Where should the company request the two certificates?

- Request both certificates in ap-southeast-2, where the application runs, and select each certificate in the distribution and in the load balancer.
- Request both certificates in US East (N. Virginia), and select each certificate in the distribution and in the load balancer.
- Request the www.example.com certificate in US East (N. Virginia) for the distribution, and the origin.example.com certificate in ap-southeast-2 for the load balancer.
- Use the default CloudFront certificate for www.example.com, and request the origin.example.com certificate in ap-southeast-2 for the load balancer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Request the www.example.com certificate in US East (N. Virginia) for the distribution, and the origin.example.com certificate in ap-southeast-2 for the load balancer.

**Deciding phrases.** "Application Load Balancer in ap-southeast-2", "CloudFront distribution for www.example.com", "certificate for origin.example.com"

**Why.** ACM certificates [must be in the same Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the resource that uses them, and [the only exception is Amazon CloudFront](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource). So the certificate of the load balancer comes from ap-southeast-2, and the certificate of the distribution from [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), from where it is [distributed to all the geographic locations](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1).

**Why not.**

- "Request both certificates in ap-southeast-2, where the application ...": The distribution reads its certificate from [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), whatever the Region of the origin, so a certificate in ap-southeast-2 does not appear in the distribution.
- "Request both certificates in US East (N. Virginia), ...": [Certificates in ACM are regional resources](../facts/acm.md#acm-certificates-regional), so the load balancer in ap-southeast-2 cannot use a certificate from US East (N. Virginia).
- "Use the default CloudFront certificate for www.example.com, and ...": For a name such as www.example.com, [the certificate must cover the alternate domain name](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cert-alternate-domain-covered-by-san), so the distribution needs its own certificate for that name.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a certificate from a third-party authority for www.example.com" instead: import it into ACM in US East (N. Virginia), because the rule covers all certificates, [including the certificates that you import](../facts/acm.md#acm-imported-regional-cloudfront).

**Takeaway.** A CloudFront certificate comes from US East (N. Virginia); a load balancer certificate comes from the Region of the load balancer.

**Review.** [CloudFront encrypts two separate connections and each one has its own setting](2-deep.md#cloudfront-encrypts-two-separate-connections-and-each-one-has-its-own-setting-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=cloudfront-q022 -->
### Question 18

A company runs an online service on Amazon EC2 instances behind Application Load Balancers in us-east-1 and us-west-2. An AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator has an endpoint group for each Region, and us-west-2 has enough capacity for all users. Users reach the service through a Route 53 alias record for the accelerator. The operations team must apply an operating system patch to the us-east-1 instances, and the patch restarts each instance. The patching must cause minimal downtime for users. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Change the Route 53 record of the service from the accelerator to the us-west-2 load balancer, wait one minute, patch the instances, and change the record back.
- Set the traffic dial of the us-east-1 endpoint group to 0, wait until the existing connections close, patch the instances, and set the dial back to 100.
- Set the traffic dial of the us-east-1 endpoint group to 0, patch the instances right away because open connections move to us-west-2, and then set the dial back.
- Launch a patched fleet behind a new load balancer in us-east-1, add it to the endpoint group, and remove the old load balancer after its connections close.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Set the traffic dial of the us-east-1 endpoint group to 0, wait until the existing connections close, patch the instances, and set the dial back to 100.

**Deciding phrases.** "enough capacity for all users", "minimal downtime for users", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** AWS describes this maintenance step: [set the traffic dial to 0](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-dec-traffic-dial-zero-cuts-off-region) for the Region, then [adjust the traffic dial to 100](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-dec-traffic-dial-zero-cuts-off-region) when the work is done. Because [the updated setting applies to only new connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-traffic-dial-new-connections-only), the team waits for open connections to close before the instances restart.

**Why not.**

- "Change the Route 53 record of the service ...": Resolvers cache the old answer [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control), so some users still reach us-east-1 through the accelerator while the instances restart.
- "Set the traffic dial of the us-east-1 endpoint ...": Open connections do not move: Global Accelerator [continues to direct traffic for established connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-established-connections-until-idle-timeout) to us-east-1, so the restarts break them.
- "Launch a patched fleet behind a new load ...": It works, but it builds a new fleet and load balancer for one patch, while a traffic dial moves new connections to us-west-2 with no new resources.

**Twin.** If the stem said "us-east-1 fails without warning" instead: health checks act without a dial change, because Global Accelerator [instantly begins directing traffic for all new connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-health-checks-standard-failover-new-connections) to another endpoint.

**Takeaway.** Planned work in one Region: turn its traffic dial down, let open connections finish, then patch.

**Review.** [Health checks and traffic dials move new connections from one Region to another](2-deep.md#health-checks-and-traffic-dials-move-new-connections-from-one-region-to-another-5-min)

</details>
